title: How To Handle Students Who Question Your Methods -methods/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the moment a student challenges a teacher's rules or procedures in front of the class, often with an accusatory tone. He warns against becoming defensive or falling back on "because I said so," arguing that such responses put the teacher at odds with the class. Instead he recommends treating the challenge as an opportunity to explain the true reason behind a policy, appealing to what he calls the power of "why." He offers sample scripted responses that reframe rules like no-calling-out or no-hallway-mobs as protections for the whole group's learning and safety. Linsin contends that many students assume teachers enjoy bossing them around simply because the reasoning was never explained. He closes by suggesting teachers openly invite such questions rather than dread them, since transparency about motives builds buy-in and proves the teacher's sincerity.
points: Reframe a student's challenge to your methods as an opportunity to explain the benefit behind the rule, not a threat to your authority.
Avoid defensive responses like "because I said so"; they set you at odds with the class.
Use scripted, empathetic explanations that connect a rule to fairness and protecting everyone's ability to learn.
Explicitly invite students to question your methods so they see your motives as transparent and student-centered.
quotes: The questions may be different, but they’re all meant to challenge your methods.
Because if you become defensive, if you cross your arms and say “because I said so” or “because I’m the teacher,” you’ll put yourself at odds with your class.
Because, in this day and age, ‘my way or the highway’ doesn’t work. It merely seals your fate to a career of stress and battling with students.
By using the power of why , and appealing to the true reason behind your decisions, you can turn such questions around.
A great many students believe that teachers enjoy bossing them around—because that’s the conclusion they draw when you don’t provide the ‘why’ of what you do.
So when you get a question that is meant to challenge you or throw you off your game, seize it. Welcome it.
It’s an approach that sets you apart and demonstrates the purity of your motives. It causes your students to swim with the tide rather than against it.
